concepts.title: API Integration and Loading States
concepts.description: Fetching data in an effect requires handling loading, success, empty and error states as requirements, and guarding against the classic race condition where a stale response arrives after a newer one.
learningObjectives: Implement the standard fetch-in-an-effect pattern, tracking loading, data, and error in state.
Explain why loading/success/empty/error are all required states, not optional polish.
Explain the stale-response race condition that occurs when a fetch-triggering prop changes quickly.
Apply the cleanup-flag and AbortController patterns to ignore or cancel a stale request.
Compare the cleanup-flag pattern to AbortController and explain when each is appropriate.

sections.heading: The Standard Pattern: Fetching Inside an Effect
sections.body: Fetching data is a **side effect**: it reaches outside rendering to talk to the network, so it belongs inside `useEffect`, not in a component's render logic. The standard shape tracks at least three pieces of state: the fetched `data`, an `isLoading` flag and an `error` value, all updated from callbacks attached to the fetch promise. The dependency array controls when a refetch happens: `[userId]` means the effect re-runs, and so refetches, whenever `userId` changes, which is what you want for a component that displays whichever user it was given. Remember that `fetch` only rejects on network failure; a 404 or 500 still resolves, so check `res.ok` and throw if you want those to reach your error state (the first example does this). Many teams use a data-fetching library or a framework's loaders instead of writing this by hand; understanding the hand-written version shows what those tools handle for you. Two UX details apply either way: when `userId` changes, decide whether to keep showing the previous data while the new request loads or to reset to a spinner (the example resets), and avoid flashing a spinner for requests that finish in a few milliseconds.

sections.heading: Loading, Success, Empty, and Error Aren't Optional Extras
sections.body:
A component that renders only the happy path, going straight to `data.map(...)` and assuming `data` is a populated array, breaks for every user, not just in a rare edge case. On the first render, before any fetch has resolved, `data` is its initial state (commonly `null` or `undefined`), and calling `.map` on that throws. That happens on every page load, during the nonzero time between mounting and the fetch resolving.

A fetch-driven component needs to render something sensible for at least four distinct states: **loading** (the fetch is in flight: show a spinner or skeleton, not an empty screen or a crash), **success** (data arrived and has entries: render it), **empty** (the fetch succeeded but there is nothing to show, such as zero search results; this is neither an error nor still loading, and deserves its own message) and **error** (the fetch failed, through a dropped connection, a 404 or a 500, and the user needs something actionable, not a blank area or an exception that takes down the page).

sections.heading: The Race Condition: A Stale Response Arriving Late
sections.body:
Consider a component that refetches whenever a prop changes, such as a profile view that refetches each time `userId` changes because the user clicks quickly through a list. Each change fires a new fetch, and responses aren't guaranteed to arrive in the order the requests were sent, so an *earlier* request can resolve *after* a *later* one, because of server load, network variance or ordinary jitter. If the effect calls `setData(result)` in every `.then` with no check that this request is still the relevant one, whichever response arrives last overwrites state, whether or not it matches what's currently selected.

For example, a user clicks profile A, then quickly B, then C. If A's request takes longer than C's (a bigger payload, a slower backend path), A's response can arrive after C's, and the screen shows profile A's data while the URL and the selected list item say C. This is a visible correctness bug that will eventually happen to real users on a real network.

sections.heading: Fixing It: Ignore (or Cancel) Stale Responses
sections.body:
There are two common fixes. The **cleanup-flag** pattern declares a local variable (commonly `isCurrent = true`) inside the effect body, and the effect's cleanup function, which React runs right before the *next* run of the effect and on unmount, flips it to `false`. Every state-setting call in the `.then`/`.catch`/`.finally` chain is guarded with `if (isCurrent)`. Because React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect, when userId changes again the *older* effect's `isCurrent` becomes false, so when its stale response arrives its guarded setters are skipped, and only the most recent request's response can update state.

The **AbortController** pattern goes a step further: create `const controller = new AbortController()` inside the effect, pass `controller.signal` to `fetch`, and call `controller.abort()` in the cleanup function. This cancels the underlying network request instead of just ignoring its result, saving bandwidth and, if the server stops work on disconnect, server effort. An aborted fetch's promise rejects with an error named `AbortError`, which is an intentional cancellation and should usually be swallowed rather than shown as an error state.

sections.heading: Choosing Between the Two Patterns
sections.body: AbortController is generally the better choice when the async operation supports cancellation (as `fetch` does), because it stops the wasted work instead of discarding the result afterward. The cleanup flag is a simpler, more universal fallback that works for any async operation, including ones with no cancellation mechanism (a `setTimeout`-based delay, a promise-based API that doesn't accept a signal). Both ensure only the most recent request's response affects state; they differ in whether the stale request is stopped or merely ignored when it finishes. Note that in development, Strict Mode runs each effect, its cleanup and the effect again on mount, so you'll see two requests; the first is aborted or ignored by exactly these patterns, and production runs the effect once.

examples.title: A Complete Fetch Component Handling All Four States
examples.explanation: Each render branch corresponds to one state: isLoading shows a spinner, a set error shows an actionable message instead of crashing, a resolved-but-empty user shows an explicit 'not found' message rather than rendering nothing or throwing, and once those checks pass the success case renders the profile. The order matters: loading is checked first because it's true throughout the fetch, before error or user are settled. isCurrent guards every setter so that if userId changes before this fetch resolves, this effect's late response can't affect state. The next example shows AbortController, which also cancels the unneeded request. (`Spinner` is assumed to exist.)

examples.title: The Same Fix Using AbortController
examples.explanation: Each time userId changes, React runs this effect's cleanup before the new effect, which calls controller.abort() on the *previous* request's controller and cancels that in-flight request instead of agreeing to ignore its result. The .catch checks err.name !== "AbortError" because an aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError, an intentional cancellation, not a failure; showing it as an error would alarm the user over something working as designed. Compared with the cleanup-flag version, this stops the wasted network work instead of letting the stale request finish and discarding the result. (The sketch omits the res.ok check and loading state from the first example.)

misconceptions.description: If I show a loading spinner while fetching, I've covered all the states this component needs to handle.
misconceptions.clarification: Loading is one of at least four states. Skipping the error state means a failed request (a dropped connection, a 404, a 500) leaves the user staring at a spinner forever, or crashes the component. Skipping the empty state means a successful-but-empty response (zero search results, a user with no orders yet) renders a confusing blank area or gets misread by the rest of the component as still loading or as an error. Loading, success, empty and error each need their own branch in the render logic.

misconceptions.description: Race conditions from fast prop changes are a rare edge case, not something that matters for a typical app.
misconceptions.clarification: Any UI where a prop driving a fetch can change before the previous fetch resolves is exposed: a type-ahead search box, quickly switching tabs or list items, paginating fast. It doesn't need an unusual network, only that response timing isn't guaranteed to match request order, which is always true over a real network. It's a correctness bug that will eventually show up for real users under normal conditions.

exercises.prompt: Assume mockFetchUser(1) resolves after 300ms with { id: 1, name: "Ada" }, and mockFetchUser(2) resolves after 50ms with { id: 2, name: "Grace" }. The component below is rendered with userId=1, then re-rendered with userId=2 about 20ms later (before the first request resolves). This effect has no protection against stale responses. Once both requests have settled, what name ends up displayed, and why?
hints: Work out the real-time order in which the two .then callbacks fire, from each mock's delay and when each request started, not the order the requests were sent.
Whichever setUser call happens last overwrites the earlier one, whichever userId that response was for.
The userId=1 request starts first but takes 300ms; the userId=2 request starts about 20ms later but takes only 50ms, resolving around the 70ms mark overall. Which .then fires later in real time?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "Ada" ends up displayed, even though userId is 2 once both requests have settled. The userId=1 request started first but has the longer delay (300ms), so its response arrives after the userId=2 response (about 70ms in). Grace is set first and briefly shown, but Ada's data arrives afterward and overwrites it, leaving a name that doesn't match the selected userId.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Timeline: the userId=1 effect starts at t=0ms and its mock resolves at t=300ms. The userId=2 effect starts around t=20ms (when the re-render with the new prop happens) and its mock resolves 50ms later, around t=70ms. So the userId=2 .then fires first, setting user to Grace, but the userId=1 .then fires later, at t=300ms, and since neither effect checks whether it's still the relevant one, its setUser(data) overwrites state with Ada. The final name is Ada, for a userId that's no longer selected. A cleanup-flag (isCurrent) guard or an AbortController prevents this by letting only the most recently started request update state.

exercises.prompt: Add a guard to the Profile component from the previous exercise so that it always displays the user matching the currently selected userId, never a stale response from an earlier request.
hints: Each effect instance needs a way to know, when its promise resolves, whether a newer effect instance has started and it should ignore what it got back.
React runs an effect's cleanup right before running that effect again. That's the moment to mark the previous instance as no longer current.
A local flag, flipped to false in cleanup and checked before calling setUser, is enough; you need AbortController only if you also want to cancel the request.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each effect instance owns an isCurrent flag, starting true. When userId changes, React runs the previous instance's cleanup before starting the new one, flipping that instance's isCurrent to false. When the userId=1 response arrives at t=300ms, its isCurrent is already false (the userId=2 effect started and triggered that cleanup around t=20ms), so its setUser(data) is skipped. Only the userId=2 instance's isCurrent is still true when its response arrives, so only it can update state, and the display matches the selected userId.

assessments.prompt: A component fetches a list of comments, and before the fetch resolves, its initial state is `comments = null`. Which statement about handling this correctly is true?
options: The component must explicitly branch on a loading state (and handle a null/undefined value) before attempting to render the list, otherwise it will throw trying to call .map on null during the first render(s).

Only the error state needs explicit handling; loading and empty states render correctly by default without any special-casing, because React skips rendering any list whose data has not yet arrived from the server.
This only matters in production, so it's safe to skip explicit handling during local development.
It's fine to render comments.map(...) directly -- React will wait for the fetch to resolve before running that line.
assessments.explanation: React doesn't pause rendering to wait for a fetch: the component renders immediately with its initial state, here null, and calling .map on null throws right away, on every load, before the fetch can resolve. So an explicit loading check (or at least a null/undefined guard) has to come before the code that assumes comments is a populated array. The “This only matters in production, so it's…” option is backwards: this crashes locally as much as in production, on first render. The “Only the error state needs explicit handling…” option is wrong: loading and empty states need their own handling just as much as error does; none of the four states renders sensibly by default.

assessments.prompt: Your `<SearchResults query={query} />` component fetches new results every time query changes as the user types quickly. Users occasionally report seeing results that don't match what's currently in the search box. Diagnose the likely cause and describe, in general terms, how you'd fix it.
assessments.modelAnswer: This is the stale-response race condition: every keystroke that changes query triggers a new fetch, and since responses aren't guaranteed to resolve in request order, an older request (for an earlier query) can resolve after a newer one. If the effect's .then calls a state setter unconditionally, the last response to arrive wins and overwrites state whether or not it matches what's typed, which is the reported symptom. The fix is to let only the most recently fired request update state: either a cleanup flag (a local isCurrent variable per effect instance, flipped to false in that effect's cleanup and checked before any setter), or an AbortController that cancels the previous in-flight request in the effect's cleanup. For type-ahead search you'd also typically debounce the input so fewer requests fire in the first place.

options: It throws a runtime error, since .map cannot be called on an array that has zero elements.

This already handles the empty case correctly, since results.map on an empty array simply produces no extra list items, which is exactly the intended behavior, and an empty list is something users already understand, so the concept recommends leaving it alone.

It renders an empty <ul> with no visible content at all, which looks indistinguishable from a bug (or a component that forgot to render anything) rather than clearly communicating "no results found" -- the fix is an explicit branch for the empty case with its own message.
It automatically falls through to the error branch, since an empty array is treated as a falsy value.
assessments.explanation: Calling .map on an empty array is legal and produces no <li> elements; it doesn't throw, ruling out the “It throws a runtime error, since .map…” option, and an array (empty or not) is truthy, ruling out the “It automatically falls through to the error…” option. The real problem is that an empty, successful result renders as a bare <ul>, which looks like something broke or hasn't loaded yet. Empty deserves its own branch and message ('No results found', for instance) instead of falling through to whatever the success branch produces for zero items.

concepts.title: CRUD and Authentication
concepts.description: A CRUD UI wires forms, lists, and API calls together into Create/Read/Update/Delete flows, and authentication on the frontend is mostly about storing a token, attaching it to requests, and protecting routes, with a security tradeoff around where that token lives.
learningObjectives: Describe what a CRUD UI is in terms of forms, lists, and API calls tied together.
Explain how the loading/success/error pattern from data fetching applies to mutations (create/update/delete), not just reads.
Explain the mechanics of frontend authentication: a token, attaching it to requests, and protecting routes.
Compare storing an auth token in localStorage versus an httpOnly cookie as a security tradeoff, not a simple right-or-wrong choice.

sections.heading: What a CRUD UI Is
sections.body:
CRUD stands for **Create, Read, Update, Delete**, the four basic operations most data-driven apps need, and a 'CRUD UI' is the forms, lists and API calls that let a user perform all four against a collection of records. **Read** is the list/detail pattern already covered: fetch and render, with loading/success/empty/error states. **Create** is a form that collects input and sends it as a POST request; on success it typically redirects to the new record's detail view or updates a list already on screen. **Update** is a form pre-filled with a record's data that sends a PUT or PATCH request with the changes. **Delete** is an action, often behind a confirmation step because it's destructive and hard to undo, that sends a DELETE request and then reflects the removal in the UI, either by refetching the list or by updating it locally.

All four share one shape across different HTTP verbs: each is a network request that can be in flight, succeed or fail, and each needs the same handling as a read. Disable the submit button and show a spinner while in flight, redirect or update the UI on success, and show an actionable error message, not a silently ignored failure, if the request fails.

sections.heading: Authentication on the Frontend
sections.body:
Authentication is a server verifying who a user is (via username and password, an OAuth flow, or similar) and then issuing something, commonly a JSON Web Token (JWT) or a session identifier, that proves the verification happened, so the user doesn't re-enter credentials on every request. The frontend's job is mostly mechanical: **store** the token after login, **attach** it to later requests (typically an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, or automatically via a cookie the browser attaches), and **react** when a request comes back unauthorized (a 401), typically by redirecting to a login page. None of this protects data by itself: the server must check the token on every request, since anything in the browser can be bypassed.

**Protecting a route** means checking, before rendering a page's content, whether there's an authenticated user, and redirecting to login if not, instead of briefly rendering protected content and finding out only when an API call fails. A route guard also needs a loading state: while the app is still determining whether a stored token is valid (say, checking it against the server on startup), it should show a loading indicator rather than redirecting to login too early or flashing real content before the check finishes.

sections.heading: Where to Put the Token: A Tradeoff
sections.body:
**localStorage** is simple: `localStorage.setItem`/`getItem` persist a value across reloads and tabs until it's cleared. The downside is that any JavaScript running on the page can read it, including a malicious script injected through an XSS (cross-site scripting) vulnerability elsewhere in the app, such as a comment field that renders user-submitted content without escaping it. If an attacker gets any script running on your page, they can read localStorage, exfiltrate the token and act as that user elsewhere.

An **httpOnly cookie**, set by the server with the `HttpOnly` flag, is the alternative: JavaScript can't read it (it doesn't appear in `document.cookie`), and the browser attaches it to matching requests automatically, so the frontend needs no code for that. This closes off the XSS read of the token itself (an injected script can still make requests as the user, which the cookie doesn't prevent). The tradeoff is two-sided: cookies bring CSRF (cross-site request forgery), since the browser attaches them to *any* request to that domain, including ones a malicious page triggers, which needs its own protections (the `SameSite` cookie attribute, CSRF tokens), and cookies can be less convenient for some cross-origin or native-mobile setups where attaching a header is simpler. A common middle path keeps a short-lived access token in memory and a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. Whichever you choose, a short token lifetime limits the damage if one leaks, and logging out should clear the stored token and, ideally, invalidate it on the server. Many real apps use localStorage successfully; the point is to know what you're trading away either way, rather than defaulting to one option without knowing why.

sections.heading: Putting It Together in a Protected CRUD Flow
sections.body: A typical flow: a login form POSTs credentials, receives a token, and stores it by whichever mechanism you chose. From then on every Create/Read/Update/Delete request attaches the token. A route guard checks for an authenticated user before rendering protected content and redirects to login if there isn't one. And if a request comes back 401, commonly because the token expired, the app clears what it stored and redirects to login, instead of leaving the user on a broken or endlessly loading page.

examples.title: A Create Form Following the Same Loading/Error Pattern as a Fetch
examples.explanation: isSubmitting disables the submit button while the request is in flight, which gives the user feedback and prevents a double submission from a second click. error shows any failure instead of silently doing nothing, which is what an empty catch block would do. onCreated hands the new comment back to the parent so it can update its list without a full refetch. Structurally this is the in-flight/success/error pattern used for reads, triggered by a form submission instead of a mount or a prop change.

examples.title: Attaching a Token and Protecting a Route
examples.explanation: apiFetch attaches the Authorization header in one place, so every request routed through it is authenticated consistently instead of repeating that logic at each call site (the header is added only when a token exists, because a header value of `undefined` would be sent as the string "undefined"). ProtectedRoute checks for a currentUser before rendering the children: while that check is resolving (isLoading) it shows a spinner rather than flashing protected content or redirecting early; once resolved it renders the page or redirects to /login. `useCurrentUser` is the context hook from the state-management exercise, and `Navigate`, `Route` and `Spinner` are assumed imports. The token is in localStorage here only to illustrate the mechanism; with an httpOnly cookie the browser would attach it automatically, removing apiFetch's header step and the XSS read described above (you'd then send `credentials: "include"` on cross-origin requests).

misconceptions.description: Storing the token in localStorage is just wrong and insecure, and no real app should do it.
misconceptions.clarification: This is a tradeoff, not a simple mistake. Many production apps use localStorage, especially when the app has strong XSS defenses (such as a framework that escapes rendered content by default). The point isn't 'never use localStorage'; it's understanding what's traded: localStorage's readability by any script on the page (a risk if an XSS hole exists anywhere) versus an httpOnly cookie's own cost (separate CSRF protections, less flexibility in some cross-origin setups).

misconceptions.description: Deleting an item from a UI list is basically instant and doesn't need any loading/error handling the way a fetch does.
misconceptions.clarification: A delete is a network request just like a GET, and it can fail (permissions changed, a network drop, a server error) or take a moment to complete. If a component removes an item from its local list optimistically, before the DELETE confirms success, and the request then fails, the UI shows something untrue about the server's state unless it handles the failure, for example by re-adding the item and showing an error. Delete needs the same in-flight/success/error treatment as Create and Update. React 19 adds Actions (`<form action={fn}>`, `useActionState`, `useFormStatus`, `useOptimistic`) that cover the pending, error and optimistic-update patterns here with less hand-written state; the underlying ideas are the same.
misconceptions.fact: A delete is a network request just like a GET, and it can fail (permissions changed, a network drop, a server error) or take a moment to complete.

exercises.prompt: A user reports that after logging in, refreshing the page always logs them back out -- even though the server confirms the token it issued is still valid for another 24 hours. What's the most likely place to look in the frontend code, and why?
hints: A full page reload discards all in-memory JavaScript state and reruns everything from scratch. What happens to a value kept only in a JS variable or component state?
Look at where the token is stored after login, and whether the app re-checks that location on startup.
If the token was never persisted anywhere that survives a reload (localStorage, or a cookie the server set), the app finds nothing when it starts again.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The most likely cause is that the token is kept only in an in-memory JS variable or component state, never persisted to localStorage or set as a cookie by the server. A reload discards in-memory state and re-runs startup from scratch, so if nothing durable was stored, the app finds nothing when it checks 'is there an authenticated user', even though the token is still valid on the server. The fix is to persist the token somewhere that survives a reload (localStorage, or an httpOnly cookie set by the server) and to read that value (or rely on the cookie being sent automatically) at startup. (Keeping the token only in memory is a deliberate choice in some designs, but then you need a way to restore the session on reload, such as a refresh cookie.)

exercises.prompt: This removes a comment from the list immediately when Delete is clicked. What happens to the UI if the DELETE request fails (e.g. the user's permissions were revoked, or the network drops), and how would you fix it?
hints: handleDelete updates the UI with setComments without waiting for or checking the result of the fetch call.
If fetch's promise rejects, or resolves with a non-ok status, does anything in this code react?
The fix is either to wait for confirmation before removing the item, or to remove it optimistically and roll back (re-add it, show an error) if the request fails.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code assumes the DELETE always succeeds and never checks the result: the comment is removed from the UI immediately and unconditionally. If the request fails, the UI shows the comment as gone while it still exists on the server, until a later refetch reveals the truth (and a rejected fetch also becomes an unhandled promise rejection). The fixed version still updates optimistically for a snappy feel, but keeps the previous list (previousComments) and rolls back to it, with an error message, if the DELETE fails, so the UI is wrong about server state only for as long as the request takes to fail.

assessments.prompt: Which statement best captures the tradeoff between storing an auth token in localStorage versus in an httpOnly cookie?
options: httpOnly cookies can't be used for authentication at all, only localStorage can.

localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on the page (a real risk if the app has an XSS vulnerability), while an httpOnly cookie can't be read by JavaScript at all but is attached to requests automatically by the browser and introduces its own CSRF considerations.
localStorage is strictly more secure because it's easier to use from JavaScript.
There's no real difference; both are equally invisible to JavaScript and equally safe.
assessments.explanation: This is a two-sided tradeoff: localStorage's convenience costs you that any script running on the page (an attacker's, via an XSS hole, included) can read it, while an httpOnly cookie closes off that read but needs separate CSRF protections since the browser attaches it automatically to matching requests, including ones triggered from elsewhere. The “localStorage is strictly more secure because it's…” and “There's no real difference; both are equally…” options understate or invert the tradeoff, and the “httpOnly cookies can't be used for authentication…” option is false: httpOnly cookies are a common, valid way to hold an auth token.

assessments.prompt: You're building the Update part of a CRUD UI for editing a blog post. A teammate says the update form doesn't need any loading or error state because 'it's just a PUT request.' Explain why they're wrong, referencing the pattern used for Create.
assessments.modelAnswer: A PUT request is still a network request, which takes time and can fail for the same reasons a POST (Create) can: a dropped connection, a validation error, a permissions issue, a timeout. With no in-flight indicator, the user gets no feedback after clicking Save and might click again, submitting a duplicate or conflicting update. With no error handling, a failed update silently does nothing from the user's view: they believe the edit was saved when it wasn't, and find out later, if ever. It's the same three-state shape (in-flight, success, error) as the Create form: disable the submit control and show feedback while the PUT is in flight, redirect or update the UI on success, and show an actionable error if it fails. PUT instead of POST changes none of that.

options: There is no bug -- currentUser is null precisely when, and only when, there's no valid session at all.
Navigate can only be rendered inside a component wrapped in React.memo, so this throws a runtime error immediately.
children is always undefined until currentUser is confirmed, so this crashes before the redirect check can even run.

While the validity check is still in progress, currentUser is momentarily null (since it hasn't resolved one way or the other yet), so this redirects every single user -- including ones with a perfectly valid session -- to /login before the check has had a chance to finish.
assessments.explanation: currentUser is null before the validity check resolves, like any state before an async operation finishes, and this component treats 'null right now' as 'definitely not authenticated', which isn't true during that startup window. Every user, including those with a valid session, is sent to /login as soon as the app loads and may land there for good, depending on how login handles an existing session: a jarring, incorrect redirect. The fix is to track and check an isLoading state from useCurrentUser too, render a loading indicator while the check is in flight, and decide to redirect only once it has completed.

concepts.title: TypeScript with React
concepts.description: TypeScript catches a whole class of prop-shape and state-shape mistakes at compile time instead of at runtime in production, but only for values you give real types to. Reaching for `any` turns the checking off for that value and everywhere it flows afterward.
learningObjectives: Explain why TypeScript pairs especially well with React's props-based component model.
Type a component's props using an interface or type, including optional and function-typed props.
Explain when TypeScript can infer a useState type versus when an explicit type argument is needed, especially for state that starts as null.
Explain what is lost when a value is typed any instead of given its real type.

sections.heading: Why TypeScript Pairs Well With React
sections.body:
Many everyday React bugs are a mismatch between what a component expects and what it was given: a forgotten required prop, a prop of the wrong type (a string where a number was expected, an object where an array was expected), a typo'd prop name, or a callback invoked with a different argument shape than the receiver assumes. In plain JavaScript/JSX none of that is caught until the code runs, and 'runs' can mean a real user hitting that code path in production, since a prop that's wrong only for some inputs may never be exercised in casual testing.

TypeScript checks the *shape* of props against a declared contract at compile time and, more usefully day to day, live in the editor as you type. 'Forgot to pass X' and 'passed the wrong shape' bugs are caught at the point of the mistake instead of surfacing later as a confusing runtime symptom (a blank render, a TypeError from deep inside unrelated-looking code) that you then trace back to its source.

sections.heading: Typing Props with an Interface or Type
Typing useState: When Inference Is Enough
sections.body:
TypeScript can usually infer a `useState` type from the initial value: `useState(0)` infers `number`, `useState("")` infers `string`, `useState(false)` infers `boolean`. No annotation is needed, since the initial value makes the type obvious.

The gap appears with state that starts empty and is populated later, most commonly `useState(null)`. Given only `null`, TypeScript infers the type `null` (under `strictNullChecks`), which rejects the code you write next, since a value typed `null` can't be set to anything else: `setUser({ name: "Ada" })` becomes a type error. The fix is an explicit type argument: `useState<User | null>(null)` says 'this will hold either a User or null', so both the initial null and a later `setUser(fetchedUser)` type-check. This is the state shape from the data-fetching concept, where a value starts unset and is populated when a fetch resolves.

sections.heading: The any Escape Hatch: What You Lose
sections.body:
When a type error is inconvenient to resolve, it's tempting to type the value as `any` to make the compiler stop complaining. But `any` doesn't mean 'infer the correct type for me'; it means 'stop type-checking this value from here on.' Any property access, method call or argument involving an `any` value is accepted with no checking.

The loss of checking doesn't stay on the line where `any` appears. If an `any` value is passed into another function, stored in another variable or returned, the receiving code loses type safety on it too, because `any` carries no information forward. One `any` can erase type safety across a much larger part of a codebase than the line it was written on. The bug you were routing around isn't fixed; it becomes invisible to the compiler and resurfaces as a runtime failure exactly where a type error would have pointed you at the problem.

examples.title: Compile-Time Errors From a Props Interface
examples.explanation: Three common mistakes are caught here: forgetting a required prop, passing the wrong primitive type, and a classic gotcha, calling a function immediately (save()) instead of passing a reference (save). TypeScript flags the last one because onClick's type expects a function, not whatever save() returns (here, assuming save returns nothing). variant's type is a union of string literals ('primary' | 'secondary'), not plain string, so a case typo like variant="Primary" would also be caught. (The block is TSX, since it contains types, although it's labeled jsx; `save` is assumed to exist.)

examples.title: Typing useState, Including State That Starts null
examples.explanation: count needs no annotation because its initial value, 0, makes number the obvious inferred type. user needs the explicit <User | null> because useState(null) alone would infer null, which would reject the setUser(data) call once the fetch resolves. The if (!user) return ... check acts as a type guard: TypeScript understands that user can't be null for the rest of the function, called narrowing, which is why user.name is allowed afterward even though user's declared type includes null. (`fetchUser` is assumed to exist.)

misconceptions.description: If TypeScript is complaining and there's no time to figure out the correct type right now, using any is a reasonable quick fix.
misconceptions.clarification: any doesn't just suppress one inconvenient error -- it removes type checking for that value everywhere it subsequently flows: into other functions, into other variables, out through return values. A safer escape hatch for a truly unknown type is unknown, which forces the code to check or narrow the value before using it, unlike any, which allows every operation unchecked. Using any by default, instead of as a rare, deliberate exception, defeats the point of typing the value.
misconceptions.fact: any doesn't just suppress one inconvenient error -- it removes type checking for that value everywhere it subsequently flows: into other functions, into other variables, out through return values.

misconceptions.description: TypeScript replaces the need to test components, since it 'checks' the code.
misconceptions.clarification: TypeScript only checks that the shapes of values match what the code declares; it doesn't know whether the logic is correct. A component can be fully type-correct (every prop the right shape, every state variable typed) and still have a wrong onClick handler, an off-by-one error, or render the wrong text, none of which is a type error. It removes one common class of bug (wrong shape, missing value) at compile time; it complements testing and doesn't replace it. Types also stop at the network boundary: `res.json()` returns `any`, so `const user: User = await res.json()` is an assertion, not a check, and a server that returns a different shape still fails at runtime. Validate untrusted data (with a schema library, for example) if the shape matters.
misconceptions.fact: TypeScript only checks that the shapes of values match what the code declares -- it has no understanding of whether the actual logic is correct.

exercises.prompt: TypeScript flags an error on the Avatar usage inside ProfileHeader below. What's wrong, and how would you fix it so the caller can still choose a size?
hints: Compare the type AvatarProps declares for size with what this call site passes.
"large" is a string literal, but size is declared as number in AvatarProps.
There are at least two valid fixes: pass a pixel number, or change AvatarProps.size to a small set of named string sizes and translate them to pixels inside Avatar.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is a type mismatch: "large" is a string, but AvatarProps declares size as number. The simplest fix is to pass a pixel value (size={64}); an equally valid alternative is to change AvatarProps.size to a union of named sizes (size: "small" | "medium" | "large") and map the names to pixels inside Avatar. TypeScript catches this before the code runs: in plain JavaScript, size="large" would silently produce width="large" in the DOM, a subtle visual bug instead of an immediate compile-time error pointing at the problem.

exercises.prompt: A teammate's pull request types a component's onSave prop as `onSave: any` because 'it always seems to work, whatever gets passed.' Explain what is given up by typing it that way, and suggest a better type.
hints: "Always seems to work" is how any looks until a caller passes something with the wrong shape and it breaks at runtime instead of compile time.
Think about what onSave should receive as an argument, and what happens to its return value, if anything. That's the type it should have.
Once onSave has a function type, a caller passing the wrong argument shape, or expecting a return value that doesn't exist, is flagged instead of accepted.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Typing onSave as any means TypeScript accepts anything as that prop (a function with the wrong parameters, a non-function) with no checking, and the lack of checking follows onSave wherever it's called or passed along inside the component. 'It always seems to work' means no caller has yet passed something incompatible that anyone noticed; any doesn't verify that stays true, it stops TypeScript from telling you when it doesn't. A better type describes what onSave receives and returns: if it saves a form's data, `onSave: (data: FormValues) => void` documents and enforces that contract, so a caller passing the wrong shape is caught immediately instead of relying on whatever cases happen to have been tried.

assessments.prompt: What's the main problem with typing a prop as any instead of giving it its actual type?
options: any makes the code run slower at runtime.
any is only permitted for props, not for state, so it causes a compile error elsewhere in the file.
any automatically converts the value to a string at runtime, which usually breaks rendering.
any disables type checking for that value entirely.
assessments.explanation: any's cost is a total loss of type checking for that value, propagating wherever it flows afterward. It has no runtime performance cost, no restriction to certain declarations, and no automatic string conversion. The “any makes the code run slower at runtime”, “any is only permitted for props…”, and “any automatically converts the value…” options describe behaviors any simply doesn't have.

assessments.prompt: Explain why useState(null) often needs an explicit type argument like useState<User | null>(null), while useState(0) doesn't need one.
assessments.modelAnswer: TypeScript infers a useState type from the initial value when that value makes the intended type clear. useState(0) infers number, since 0 is a number and the state presumably holds numbers. useState(null) has only null to infer from, so TypeScript infers the narrowest type, literally null, with nothing suggesting the state will hold anything else. That type then rejects the code usually written next, such as setUser(fetchedUserObject) once an API call resolves, because a value typed null can't become anything else. An explicit type argument, useState<User | null>(null), states the intended type up front, a User or null, so both the initial null and the later set to a User type-check.

options: duration automatically becomes the string "undefined" cast to a number, which avoids any rendering issue.
duration is undefined, and TypeScript does not flag this as an error.
duration is 0, and TypeScript flags nothing, since an optional numeric prop automatically defaults to its type's zero value.
TypeScript throws a compile-time error here, since every prop declared in an interface must always be explicitly passed by every caller, optional or not.
assessments.explanation: The ? in duration?: number only tells TypeScript that a caller may omit this prop, so <Alert message="Saved!" /> compiles, because duration is optional. Marking something optional doesn't produce a fallback at runtime; without a default in the destructuring (like duration = 3000), duration is undefined inside Alert. React renders undefined as nothing, so the output would read "(visible for ms)", which is unhelpful. TypeScript catches shape mismatches (the wrong type, an omitted required prop), not missing runtime defaults for props you've said may be absent.

concepts.title: Testing React Components
concepts.description: React's testing ecosystem converged on testing behavior a user would experience rather than implementation details, and React Testing Library's queries (by role, label and visible text) are built to push you that way.
learningObjectives: Explain the 'test behavior, not implementation details' philosophy and why it matters across refactors.
Describe the React Testing Library mental model of querying the rendered output the way a user would.
Contrast a brittle test (querying by CSS class) with a resilient one (querying by role/text) and explain why one survives a refactor the other doesn't.
Write a test that simulates a user interaction and asserts on the resulting visible output.

sections.heading: Test Behavior, Not Implementation Details
sections.body:
The React testing ecosystem converged on one philosophy: tests should verify what a user experiences (what appears on screen, what happens after they click or type) rather than internal mechanics like which state variable holds a value, whether a hook fired, or what an internal method is named.

The reasoning is practical: implementation details change constantly in correct refactors, such as renaming a state variable, switching from useState to useReducer, or extracting logic into a custom hook. None of that changes anything a user can observe. If tests are coupled to those details, every such refactor breaks tests that found nothing wrong with the app: a false alarm. False alarms erode a suite's usefulness: once a team learns that red tests often mean 'harmless refactor noise', people start ignoring failures, and the tests stop doing their job.

sections.heading: The Testing Library Model: Query Like a User
sections.body:
React Testing Library's central idea is to find elements the way a person, or assistive technology like a screen reader, would: by visible text, by accessible role, by an associated label. Not through implementation details like a CSS class that exists for styling, or a component's internal props or instance.

In practice that gives a rough priority order: prefer `getByRole("button", { name: "Submit" })`, `getByLabelText("Email")` or `getByText("Welcome back")` over anything like `container.querySelector(".some-class")`. The ordering is about more than resilience; it doubles as a rough accessibility check. If `getByRole("button", { name: "Submit" })` can't find your submit button, a screen reader user may not find it either, since both rely on the same accessible structure of the markup.

sections.heading: Brittle vs. Resilient
sections.body:
Imagine a login form whose submit button has the class `.btn-primary`, and a test that finds it with `document.querySelector(".btn-primary")`. A visual redesign renames the class to `.button--primary`; what the button does and displays is unchanged, only a styling hook's name. The class-based test breaks even though behavior is the same, a false failure that costs someone time investigating something that was never broken.

A test that finds the button with `screen.getByRole("button", { name: /log in/i })` keeps passing through the same redesign, because the button's role (button) and visible name ('Log In') didn't change; only a presentational detail did, and the resilient test never depended on it.

sections.heading: What This Looks Like in Practice
sections.body:
Interactions are simulated with `fireEvent` or `userEvent` (clicking, typing), and assertions are made on the visible output: text appearing or disappearing, an input's displayed value changing. `userEvent` (from `@testing-library/user-event`) is generally preferred because it fires the full sequence of events a real interaction produces (pointer, focus, key events); in v14 its methods are async (`await user.click(...)`), and you create it with `userEvent.setup()`. For content that appears after async work, use `findBy*` queries or `waitFor`. Components that fetch data are usually tested by intercepting the network rather than mocking `fetch` or the component's internals; Mock Service Worker (MSW) is a common choice, so the component runs exactly as it would in the browser. What's absent is any assertion on a component's internal state.

That absence is deliberate. That a test can't tell from the outside whether a component uses useState or useReducer is a feature: a user can't observe that choice either, so a test that represents what a user experiences shouldn't see it or care about it.

examples.title: Brittle CSS-Class Query vs. Resilient Role/Text Query
examples.explanation: If a redesign renames .submit-btn to .cta-button, or moves the error text into a differently classed element, the brittle test breaks even though LoginForm's behavior (clicking 'Log In' without a password shows this message) hasn't changed. The resilient version finds the button by role and visible label, and the error by the text a user would read; neither depends on a CSS class, so a visual restructuring leaves it passing, as it should. (`toBeInTheDocument` comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom`, and `render`, `screen` and `fireEvent` from `@testing-library/react`.)

examples.title: Testing an Interaction Without Touching Internal State
examples.explanation: This test never touches SearchableList's internal state, however the filter text is held or the filtering is implemented. It interacts with the input as a user would (found by role and label, then typed into) and asserts on what is visible afterward. queryByText (which returns null if nothing matches) is used to assert something is absent, because getByText (which throws if nothing matches) would throw before the assertion ran; Testing Library provides both variants for these two purposes.

misconceptions.description: A good test should check that a component's internal state updated correctly after an interaction.
misconceptions.clarification: Internal state is an implementation detail invisible to users. Testing it directly, for instance by exposing internals just to test them, couples the test to how the component is built today, so a behavior-preserving refactor (changing the state shape, splitting logic into a different hook) breaks the test for no reason. Assert on the rendered outcome instead: that's what has to stay correct for users, however it's implemented underneath.
misconceptions.fact: Internal state is an implementation detail invisible to actual users.

misconceptions.description: getByRole and similar Testing Library queries are just a more verbose way to do the same thing document.querySelector does.
misconceptions.clarification: They aren't equivalent even when they find the same element. Role- and label-based queries succeed only when the markup is accessible (correct semantic elements, appropriate ARIA attributes, real associated labels), so a passing getByRole test is some baseline evidence that the UI works with assistive technology, not only with a mouse and eyes. A className selector can find any div, whether or not a screen reader could make sense of it.

exercises.prompt: A code review comment says: 'This test does expect(wrapper.find(".modal-overlay").length).toBe(1) to check the modal opened -- can you make this more resilient?' Describe, in words, a different approach to the assertion, and explain what makes your version survive a future CSS refactor that the original wouldn't.
hints: The original query is coupled to a CSS class. What does a user perceive when a modal opens, that has nothing to do with any class name?
A modal is typically an accessible dialog with visible text inside it. What role or text could you query for instead?
Think about what changes in a purely visual or CSS refactor, and confirm your query doesn't depend on any of it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Instead of counting elements with a CSS class, query for something a user perceives when the modal opens: screen.getByRole("dialog") if the modal has an accessible dialog role, or screen.getByText(...) for visible text that appears only when it's open, then assert it's present with toBeInTheDocument(). This survives a CSS refactor because renaming or restructuring .modal-overlay doesn't change the modal's role or visible text, which come from the markup's semantics and content. The original breaks under that refactor because .modal-overlay is the detail being renamed, even though the modal opens and behaves the same for the user. (`wrapper.find` is Enzyme syntax; Enzyme has no official adapter beyond React 17, one reason the ecosystem moved to Testing Library.)

exercises.prompt: Given the CartWidget component below, write a test using React Testing Library-style queries that verifies clicking the 'Add to Cart' button updates the visible item count, without asserting on any internal state directly.
hints: Find the button the way a user would, by its visible label, not by a class or internal ref.
After the click, assert on the text now visible on screen, not on a state variable inside CartWidget.
screen.getByText can match the exact string that should now be showing, e.g. 'Items in cart: 1'.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This test finds the button by role and visible name, fires a click, and asserts on the visible text before and after. It never reaches into CartWidget's count state through an instance, a hook value or a ref. If CartWidget later changed from useState to useReducer, or renamed count to itemCount, the test would pass unchanged, because none of that is visible to a user or checked by the test. (With user-event you'd write `await user.click(...)` after `const user = userEvent.setup()`.)

assessments.prompt: Why does React Testing Library encourage querying by role and accessible text/label instead of by CSS class name?
options: Role and label queries are simply an alias for querySelector with identical behavior under the hood.
CSS-class-based queries are slower to execute in the test runner.

Querying by role/label matches how a real user (including one using assistive technology) actually finds things on screen, so tests track real behavior and stay valid across purely visual refactors that change classes without changing what's rendered semantically.
CSS classes are not supported by the DOM APIs that Testing Library depends on.
assessments.explanation: The reasoning is about what a query represents, not execution speed or DOM API support (both non-issues; the “CSS-class-based queries are slower to execute…” and “CSS classes are not supported…” options describe problems that don't exist). Role/label queries track the accessible structure a user (or their assistive technology) relies on, so they stay valid through refactors that only change styling classes, while a className query breaks when the class is renamed for visual reasons. The “Role and label queries are simply…” option is false: role/label queries check accessible semantics, which querySelector knows nothing about.

assessments.prompt: A test suite has several tests asserting on a component's internal state values directly, by reaching into a returned hook's internals or a component instance. Explain, in terms of what happens during a refactor, why this is considered an anti-pattern in the React Testing Library philosophy.
assessments.modelAnswer: Internal state values (which hook holds them, what they're named, how they're structured) are implementation details a user of the rendered page can't observe or care about. A test that asserts on them is coupled to how the component is built today. If a later, valid refactor changes any of that (useState to useReducer, logic split into a differently named custom hook, a different internal structure) without changing what the component looks like or does, the refactor breaks these tests anyway. That's a false failure: the tests report a problem that doesn't exist for any user, and repeated false failures train a team to distrust red results, which undermines the suite. Testing the rendered outcome (what text appears, what happens after a simulated click) ties tests to behavior that has to stay correct whatever the implementation, so they fail only when something a user would notice has broken.

assessments.prompt: A test wants to assert that "Apple" is NOT present in the rendered output after a list has been filtered. Using `screen.getByText("Apple")` for this assertion (e.g. wrapped in a `.not.toBeInTheDocument()` expectation) would be a mistake. Why?
options: getByText throws an error immediately if no matching element is found, so the test would fail with a thrown error before ever reaching the intended "not present" assertion -- queryByText, which returns null instead of throwing, is the correct tool for asserting something is absent.
getByText and queryByText behave identically in every situation, so there's no meaningful difference to worry about here.
getByText is case-sensitive in a way that would fail to match "Apple" for unrelated reasons.
getByText only works for headings, not for list items like "Apple".
assessments.explanation: getByText is for when you expect a match to exist: if nothing matches, it throws immediately, which fails the test before an assertion about absence can run. queryByText is for the opposite case: it returns null when nothing matches, which is what a `.not.toBeInTheDocument()` assertion needs. That's why Testing Library provides both variants: get* for 'this should exist, fail loudly if it doesn't', and query* for 'this might legitimately not exist, and that's fine to check'.

concepts.title: Performance Optimization
concepts.description: Identifying unnecessary re-renders starts with profiling, not guessing, and tools like React.memo, useCallback/useMemo and code splitting each solve a specific, measured problem. Reaching for them by default adds complexity without a guaranteed benefit.
learningObjectives: Explain why profiling with React DevTools should come before any optimization attempt.
Explain what React.memo does and when skipping a re-render matters.
Explain why passing a new inline function or object prop on every render defeats React.memo, and how useCallback/useMemo fix it.
Describe code splitting and lazy loading as a way to reduce initial bundle size, distinct from reducing re-renders.
Explain the cost of premature optimization and why profiling should precede and follow any optimization attempt.

sections.heading: Measure First: The React DevTools Profiler
sections.body:
Before optimizing anything, get evidence of what's slow and why, not a guess that 'this component seems like it would be expensive.' The React DevTools Profiler records renders as they happen and shows which components rendered, how long each took, and (if you enable 'Record why each component rendered while profiling' in its settings) *why* each one rendered: props changed, state changed, a parent re-rendered, a context value changed. That turns 'I have a hunch this is slow' into a measured target: this component, re-rendering this often, taking this long, for this reason. Profile a production build when you can, since development builds are slower and add checks.

The sequence: profile, find a measured bottleneck, optimize that thing, then profile again to confirm it helped. Some slow screens aren't re-render problems at all: a list of thousands of rows is slow because of the DOM nodes, and the fix is windowing (rendering only the visible rows, with a library such as react-window), while an expensive update that blocks typing can be marked non-urgent with `useTransition` or `useDeferredValue`. Adding memoization everywhere up front is a guess dressed up as optimization, and guesses are often wrong about where the cost in a React app lives.

sections.heading: React.memo: Skipping Re-renders for Unchanged Props
sections.body: `React.memo` wraps a component so React can skip re-rendering it when its props are the same, reference for reference, as on the previous render (a shallow, key-by-key comparison), even if its parent just re-rendered for an unrelated reason. It helps for a component that is expensive to render and often receives the same props while its parent updates for other reasons. Wrapping a component that's cheap to render, or whose props change on nearly every parent render anyway, buys little, since there's rarely a re-render to skip.

sections.heading: Why memo Needs useCallback/useMemo to Actually Work
sections.body:
Here's the gotcha that ties back to useCallback and useMemo: memo's comparison is shallow, so a new function or object *literal* created on every parent render is a different reference every time, even if its behavior or content is identical. `<ExpensiveChild onClick={() => doThing()} />` hands ExpensiveChild a new onClick on every render of its parent, however stable `doThing` is. memo's comparison sees 'this prop changed' each time and ExpensiveChild re-renders anyway, with no warning that the memo did nothing. The same applies to `children`: JSX you pass between a component's tags is a new element object on every parent render, so a memoized component that receives children also re-renders.

The fix is what the prerequisite concept covers: wrap the callback in `useCallback` (and any object or array literal prop in `useMemo`) in the parent, so the same reference is reused across renders where its dependencies haven't changed. That's why useMemo/useCallback and React.memo are usually discussed together: for props passed into a memoized component, memo does little without them in this very common scenario. (The React Compiler can add much of this memoization automatically in projects that use it.)

sections.heading: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
sections.body:
This is a different problem from re-renders: reducing how much JavaScript the browser must download and parse before the app is usable, rather than reducing work on later renders. `React.lazy(() => import("./HeavyChart"))` combined with `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` defers fetching a component's code until it's needed (a route only some visitors visit, or a heavy charting library behind a tab most users never open) instead of bundling it into the initial JS payload every visitor downloads.

For example, a 2MB charting library in the main bundle makes every visitor pay the download and parse cost on first load, including those who never open the tab that uses it. Lazy-loading it means only visitors who navigate to that tab pay, once, when it's needed. The route level is the most common place to split, since a route is a natural boundary for a user waiting briefly.

sections.heading: Premature Optimization Has a Cost
sections.body:
Memoizing everything by default (every component in memo, every function in useCallback, every derived value in useMemo, without measuring) isn't free. Each memoization costs a comparison or cache check on every render; each adds a dependency array that has to stay correct, an easy source of subtle bugs when a dependency is missed; and each adds indirection that makes the code harder to read, for a benefit that may be marginal or nil on a component that was never slow.

React re-rendering a simple component is usually very fast, fast enough that memoizing it defensively can cost more than the render it avoids, and often makes no measurable difference while making the code harder to follow. Also check the cheaper fixes first: state that lives higher than it needs to is a common cause of wide re-renders, and moving it down (or passing expensive subtrees as `children`) can remove the problem without any memoization. The sequence is still: profile, identify a bottleneck backed by numbers, optimize that thing, and re-measure to confirm it helped, instead of memoizing everywhere 'just in case'.

examples.title: React.memo Paired With useCallback
examples.explanation: If handleSelect were recreated on every render (the commented-out version), every ExpensiveRow would receive a 'new' onSelect each time ItemList re-rendered for any reason, so React.memo's comparison would report changed props and every row would re-render despite the memo. With useCallback (an empty dependency array, since handleSelect closes over nothing that changes), the same function reference is reused across renders, so memo sees 'same props' for rows whose item prop didn't change, and the console.log fires only for rows whose item changed. This assumes the `items` and their objects keep their identity between renders (they come from props here); freshly built item objects would defeat the memo too.

examples.title: Lazy Loading a Heavy Component
examples.explanation: HeavyChart's JavaScript (and the charting library it depends on) is split into its own bundle chunk by the build tool, and that chunk is fetched only when showChart becomes true and React needs to render HeavyChart, not as part of the initial bundle every visitor downloads whether or not they click the button. Suspense's fallback covers the gap while the chunk loads, the loading-state idea from data fetching applied to code instead of data.

misconceptions.description: Wrapping a component in React.memo always makes it faster, so it's safe to wrap everything in memo by default.
misconceptions.clarification: memo helps only when a component would otherwise re-render with unchanged props and that re-render is expensive enough to matter. For a cheap component, the shallow comparison memo performs on every render can cost about as much as re-rendering, so wrapping everything can make things marginally slower while making the code harder to read. It's a tool for a measured bottleneck, not a default.

misconceptions.description: Since ExpensiveChild is wrapped in React.memo, passing it a new inline arrow function or object literal as a prop is fine -- memo will handle it.
misconceptions.clarification: memo's shallow comparison sees a new function or object literal as a different value on every render, purely because it's a different reference in memory. memo doesn't know that the function's behavior is identical to last time; it compares references, not behavior or content. Any inline () => ... or { ... } literal passed as a prop into a memoized component defeats the memoization for that prop, with no warning, which is why such props need stabilizing with useCallback or useMemo in the parent for memo to have an effect.

exercises.prompt: Row is wrapped in React.memo. Clicking on row 'B' calls handleSelect, which triggers a state update and causes List to re-render. handleSelect is a plain function declaration, not wrapped in useCallback. Given that, which Row components log a new 'render:' line as a result of this one click -- just B, or all three?
hints: Row is wrapped in React.memo, which skips re-rendering when props are reference-equal to last time. Check every prop each Row receives, not just item.
handleSelect is a new function each time List's function body runs, including on this re-render triggered by the click.
Since onSelect is a new reference every render for all three rows, not just the clicked one, what does memo's comparison conclude about each Row's props?
exercises.expectedAnswer: All three Row components log a new 'render:' line, not just B. List re-declares handleSelect on every render, so every Row's onSelect prop is a new reference after the click, whichever row was clicked. memo's comparison sees changed props for A, B and C alike, and all three re-render. (This is the first click: the state goes from null to 2, which triggers the render. Clicking B again would set the same value and React would skip re-rendering List.)
exercises.solutionExplanation: handleSelect is a plain function declaration inside List's body, so a new function object is created every time List runs, including this re-render triggered by clicking B. That new handleSelect is passed as onSelect to every Row, so all three receive a prop with a different reference than last render, even though item (defined outside List, so stable) is the same for A and C. React.memo checks every prop, and since onSelect differs for all three, all three re-render and console.log fires for A, B and C. Wrapping handleSelect in useCallback (with an empty dependency array, since it only calls setSelectedId, which is stable across renders) would give every Row the same onSelect reference across renders, letting memo skip A, B and C when nothing they receive changed.

exercises.prompt: Fix the List component from the previous exercise so that React.memo can skip re-rendering the rows when one is clicked, instead of all three re-rendering every time.
hints: The fix is the pairing already covered: stabilize the function reference passed as a prop into the memoized component.
Wrap handleSelect in useCallback so the same function reference is reused across renders whose dependencies haven't changed.
handleSelect only calls setSelectedId, which React guarantees is stable across renders, so its dependency array can be empty.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Wrapping handleSelect in useCallback with an empty dependency array reuses the same function across every render of List, since setSelectedId is stable and nothing else is captured. When B is clicked and List re-renders, every Row receives the same onSelect and the same item (the items array is defined outside List), so memo sees unchanged props and skips all three rows. None of them re-render here because selectedId isn't passed down; if Row received an isSelected prop, only the rows whose isSelected changed would re-render. It's the gotcha from the explanation: memo alone wasn't enough, because the function prop kept changing reference underneath it, and the item objects must be stable too (here, hoisted out of the component).

assessments.prompt: A component is wrapped in React.memo, but profiling shows it still re-renders every time its parent re-renders, even though nothing about what it looks like on screen ever changes. What's the most likely cause?
options: The component has too many hooks for memo to track correctly.

One or more props passed to it are new object, array, or function references on every parent render (such as an inline arrow function or object literal), which defeats memo's shallow reference comparison even though their actual content is unchanged.
memo only works if the component has no children.
React.memo doesn't work on function components, only class components.
assessments.explanation: This is the memo-plus-inline-prop gotcha: a new function or object literal created on every parent render is a different reference every time, and memo's shallow comparison treats that as changed props, whether or not the content or behavior is identical. React.memo works perfectly well on function components (the “React.memo doesn't work on function components, only class components” option is false), has no limit related to hook count (the “The component has too many hooks…” option is false), and has no restriction related to children (the “memo only works if the component has no children” option is false) -- none of those describe real constraints of memo.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer wraps every single component in the app with React.memo and every function passed as a prop with useCallback, 'to be safe.' Explain, using the idea of measuring first, why this might not actually be a good idea, even if it doesn't break anything functionally.
assessments.modelAnswer: Wrapping everything defensively skips the step that justifies memo/useCallback in the first place: measuring, with the React DevTools Profiler or similar, whether a component's re-renders are both frequent and expensive enough to matter. Without it, most of the memoization lands on components that were already cheap to re-render, where its cost (a shallow prop comparison on every render, a dependency array to maintain) can match or exceed the re-render it prevents. The result is no real benefit, code that's harder to read, and a new class of bug (a wrong or stale dependency array). The productive order is the reverse: profile under realistic conditions, find components that re-render often and take meaningful time, apply memo/useCallback/useMemo to those, and profile again to confirm it helped, instead of applying it everywhere on the assumption that it can only help.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: "Since AnalyticsPage loads a 2MB charting library and feels slow to first show anything, let's wrap the chart component in React.memo to fix it." Why is React.memo the wrong tool for the specific problem being described?
options: React.memo would actually make the initial load slower, since wrapping a component in it triggers an extra network request of its own.
React.memo cannot be applied to any component that internally uses a third-party charting library.

React.memo only affects whether an already-loaded component skips re-rendering on subsequent updates -- it does nothing about how much JavaScript has to be downloaded and parsed before the app becomes interactive in the first place, which is what's actually causing the slow initial load. Code splitting/lazy loading (React.lazy plus Suspense) is the tool built for that.
React.memo and code splitting are two different names for the exact same underlying mechanism, so either one would fix this equally well.
assessments.explanation: A slow initial load caused by a large library's JS being downloaded and parsed is a bundle-size problem, not a re-render problem, and memo has nothing to say about bundle size; it only decides whether to skip re-rendering a component that's already loaded and mounted. memo wouldn't reduce the JS shipped on first load by a byte. Code splitting via React.lazy and Suspense is the tool for this problem, since it defers fetching the heavy component's code until it's needed instead of bundling it into what every visitor downloads upfront.

concepts.title: Deployment and Architecture
concepts.description: Most React apps ship through a build step into static assets with build-time environment configuration, benefit from a feature-based folder structure as they grow, and choose between client-side and server-side rendering as a tradeoff rather than a default.
learningObjectives: Explain what the build step does to source code before it's deployed.
Explain how build-time environment variables configure the same codebase differently per environment, and their limits.
Contrast feature-based folder architecture with organizing by file type, and explain why the former scales better.
Explain the tradeoffs between client-side rendering and server-side rendering.

sections.heading: The Build Step: From Source to Static Assets
sections.body:
Most React apps aren't shipped as the JSX and modern JavaScript you write. A build tool (Vite, webpack and similar) runs a **build step** that bundles the app's JavaScript, CSS and dependencies into fewer optimized files; transpiles JSX and newer syntax into something every target browser can run; minifies the result (stripping whitespace, shortening variable names) to reduce file size; and often splits the output into chunks, the mechanism behind the lazy-loading pattern from the performance concept.

The output is a folder of static HTML/CSS/JS files, deployed to a server or CDN. 'Static' means the server hands these pre-built files out as-is; it doesn't run React code to produce them on the fly. That matters when contrasted with server-side rendering, where a server runs React code on each request. Because deployed filenames usually contain a content hash, they can be cached for a long time while `index.html` stays short-lived, so a new deploy reaches users.

sections.heading: Environment-Specific Configuration
sections.body:
The same codebase usually has to behave differently depending on where it runs: `http://localhost:3000/api` locally, a staging URL in staging, the production API in production. This is commonly handled with **build-time environment variables**: `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` in Vite (only variables prefixed `VITE_` are exposed to the client code), or `process.env.REACT_APP_API_URL` in older Create React App setups (CRA is now deprecated). They are substituted into the built JS files at build time, not read from the server's runtime environment the way a backend app's variables are. So you generally produce a distinct build per environment, rather than one build that decides its own API URL by inspecting where it runs.

A security point follows: anything baked into a frontend build this way is visible to anyone who opens dev tools and reads the shipped JS. 'Build-time environment variable' doesn't mean 'hidden' in a frontend app, as it might for server-side configuration. Use it for configuration (a base API URL, a public feature flag), never for secrets that must stay private, like an API key that must not be exposed to end users.

sections.heading: Feature-Based Folder Architecture
sections.body:
As an app grows, file organization starts to matter. Organizing by **file type** groups files into folders like `components/`, `hooks/` and `styles/`, each holding files from every feature, mixed together. Organizing by **feature** groups everything related to one feature together: `features/checkout/{CheckoutForm.jsx, useCheckout.js, checkout.css}`, `features/profile/{...}`, and so on.

The feature-based layout tends to scale better because the folder structure makes the *relationships between files* explicit. In a type-based layout with 200 components, the structure doesn't tell you which components belong to which feature, or which are safe to change or delete together; that knowledge lives in people's heads or scattered documentation. A `features/checkout/` folder shows the likely blast radius of a checkout change at a glance. It isn't a rule every project needs from day one (a small app with five components gains little from the ceremony); it responds to a growth problem, as Context or a state-management library earns its keep only once state gets complex enough to need it. A common companion rule is to import across features only through each feature's public entry file, so features don't reach into each other's internals.

sections.heading: CSR vs. SSR: A Brief Framing
sections.body:
Everything so far has assumed **client-side rendering (CSR)**: the server sends a nearly empty HTML shell (commonly just `
`) plus a JS bundle, and the browser downloads and runs the JS, which builds and inserts the UI. There's a measurable gap between 'the page arrives' and 'the page has visible content', and a crawler or link-preview bot that doesn't execute JavaScript may see only the empty shell. **Server-side rendering (SSR)** works differently: the server runs the React components and sends back HTML that already contains visible content, so the browser has something to show immediately. The JS bundle is still sent and run afterward to 'hydrate' that markup, attaching event handlers so it becomes interactive. Each approach has tradeoffs. CSR's JS payload can mean slower time to first visible content, especially on slow connections or devices, but needs only simple infrastructure (a static file server or CDN). SSR gives faster initial content and generally better default SEO and link previews, but needs a server running React on every request (or a pre-rendering or caching layer), which is more infrastructure to run and maintain. Rendering the HTML once at build time (static site generation) sits between the two for content that doesn't change per request. Next.js is the common way to get SSR in the React ecosystem, and recent React versions add Server Components, which render on the server and ship no component JS to the browser; this lesson doesn't go into those APIs.

examples.title: The Same Source Code, Configured Differently Per Build
