examples.explanation: The same line of source, import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, resolves to a different literal string depending on which build was run: the build tool substitutes the value at build time and bakes it into the output JS, instead of reading it from the server at request time as a backend app's environment variable would. A production build made with the wrong .env file active would point the deployed app at the wrong backend, with no runtime check to catch the mismatch. The value is fixed when the build runs and stays that way until a new build is deployed. (The two env files are shown as one block for comparison; they are separate files, and `fetch` here assumes the code runs inside a function.)

examples.title: Type-Based vs. Feature-Based Folder Structure
examples.code:
// Type-based (relationships between files are invisible in the structure):
src/
  components/
    CheckoutForm.jsx
    ProfileCard.jsx
    CheckoutSummary.jsx
    ProfileSettings.jsx
  hooks/
    useCheckout.js
    useProfile.js
  styles/
    checkout.css
    profile.css

// Feature-based (everything one feature needs lives together):
src/
  features/
    checkout/
      CheckoutForm.jsx
      CheckoutSummary.jsx
      useCheckout.js
      checkout.css
    profile/
      ProfileCard.jsx
      ProfileSettings.jsx
      useProfile.js
      profile.css
examples.explanation: In the type-based layout, checkout code is scattered across three top-level folders, next to unrelated profile files. Deleting or substantially changing the checkout feature means touching or checking components/, hooks/ and styles/, and nothing in the structure signals that CheckoutForm.jsx and useCheckout.js are related. In the feature-based layout the relationship is explicit: everything checkout needs lives in features/checkout/, so a change or deletion has a contained blast radius, and a new contributor can see what belongs together without cross-referencing parallel folders.

misconceptions.description: Since API keys are read from environment variables and never appear as literal strings in the source code, they're safe to use as build-time env vars in a frontend app.
misconceptions.clarification: Anything baked into a frontend build via build-time environment variables is embedded in the JS files the browser downloads, visible to anyone who inspects the bundle, however it was written in the original source. Build-time env vars suit non-secret configuration (a base API URL, a public feature flag) that any user may see. Real secrets belong on a server the frontend calls, never in a frontend build. If the browser needs data that requires a secret key, have your own backend make that call and expose a narrow endpoint instead. Variables without the `VITE_` prefix are not exposed to client code by Vite, which is a guard against leaking server-only values by accident, but anything you do prefix is public.

misconceptions.description: Server-side rendering means React doesn't run in the browser at all for that page.
misconceptions.clarification: SSR generates the initial HTML on the server so there's visible content immediately, but the JS bundle is still sent to and run in the browser afterward (hydration) to attach event handlers and make the markup interactive. Without hydration the page would look right but buttons and inputs wouldn't respond. SSR changes where the first render happens and what the first response contains; React still runs in the browser for that page.

exercises.prompt: Your team's app has grown to 40 components, and finding all the files related to the 'notifications' feature currently means checking components/, hooks/, utils/, and styles/, since the app is organized by file type. What would reorganizing by feature look like for this specific case, and what problem would it solve?
hints: Identify every file across the type-based folders that is about notifications, whichever folder it lives in.
A feature-based reorganization would gather all of those specific files into one place.
Think about what changes for someone who needs to modify or delete the notifications feature after the reorganization.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Reorganizing by feature means creating a features/notifications/ folder and moving every notifications component, hook, utility and style file now scattered across components/, hooks/, utils/ and styles/ into it. Instead of having to know, or find by searching, that notifications code lives in four unrelated top-level folders, everything the feature needs is in one place. Someone modifying or removing the feature can see its full footprint in one folder instead of hunting through parallel type-based folders and hoping nothing was missed. Code used by several features (a generic Button, a date utility) stays in a shared folder. Reorganizing is cheap with an editor that updates imports automatically, so do it in one focused change, separate from behavior changes, to keep the diff reviewable.

exercises.prompt: A deployed production build is making API calls to http://localhost:3000/api, which obviously doesn't exist for real users. The code uses import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, and this worked fine locally. What's the most likely cause, and how would you actually fix it?
hints: Environment variables like VITE_API_URL are substituted at build time and baked into the output files, not read from the environment the running server happens to be in.
Consider which .env file (or equivalent build configuration) was active when the production build was run for this deployment.
If the build used a development env file, or no production configuration existed, what value would VITE_API_URL be baked in as, and can that be fixed without a new build?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The most likely cause is that the production build ran with the development value in effect (a build made with the wrong mode or an overriding variable, or no production env configuration existed), so VITE_API_URL was baked in as the localhost value. The substitution happens once, at build time, and is fixed in the resulting JS, so editing a config file on the deployed server can't fix it; the wrong value is already in the shipped bundle. The fix is to ensure a production env file (or build configuration) with the correct API URL is active when the build for that target is produced, then rebuild and redeploy. Editing anything on the running server has no effect on values already baked into the JS. (By default `vite build` uses `.env.production`, so also check CI environment variables, which can override env files.)

assessments.prompt: A React app's production build makes a request to the wrong API URL because a build-time environment variable held the wrong value. Which statement correctly explains why this can't be fixed by just editing a config file on the already-deployed server?
options: Those values are substituted into the JS bundle at build time, so fixing one requires a rebuild.
The fix just requires restarting the static file server, which re-reads environment variables automatically on restart.
Frontend apps don't actually support environment-specific configuration at all.
Environment variables in frontend builds are read fresh from the browser's own environment on every page load, so simply refreshing the page would fix it.
assessments.explanation: Build-time environment variables are substituted into the JS at the moment the build runs, so the value is fixed inside the shipped files; the only way to change it is to produce and deploy a new build with the correct value. The “Frontend apps don't actually support environment-specific configuration at all”, “The fix just requires restarting the static…”, and “Environment variables in frontend builds are read…” options each describe a mechanism that isn't how build-time environment variables work; none would affect a value already baked into files that have been built and deployed.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone deciding between a purely client-side-rendered React app and a server-side-rendered one, the tradeoff involved, beyond 'SSR is better for SEO.'
assessments.modelAnswer: With client-side rendering, the server's initial response is a nearly empty HTML shell plus a JS bundle; the browser must download and execute the JS before real content appears, which creates a gap between the page arriving and having visible content (worse on slow connections or devices), and a crawler or link-preview bot that doesn't execute JS may see only the empty shell, which is the source of the common SEO concern. The upside is simple infrastructure: a static file server or CDN is enough, since nothing runs application code per request. With server-side rendering, the server runs the React components and sends HTML that already contains visible content, so there's no gap, and crawlers see real content without executing JS. The cost is that a server (or a pre-rendering or caching layer) must run React code per request instead of handing out static files, which is more infrastructure to run, scale and maintain. Neither is simply 'better': CSR trades initial content speed and default SEO for infrastructure simplicity, and SSR trades that simplicity for faster initial content and better default SEO. Next.js is the most common way to get SSR in the React ecosystem.

assessments.prompt: An SSR page's initial HTML response already shows a fully rendered product list. The instant the page appears, a user clicks "Add to Cart" on the first visible item, but for a brief moment nothing visibly happens. What's the most likely explanation?
options: SSR pages never support click handlers at all; only purely client-side-rendered apps can ever respond to click events.
The server has to fully re-render the entire page from scratch in response to every click, which explains the brief delay.

This indicates a bug specific to this app; a correctly built SSR page is otherwise always fully interactive the instant any content becomes visible, so the delay must come from an event handler that was attached to the wrong element by mistake in this app's own code.

The JS bundle needed to hydrate the page (attaching real event handlers to the already-rendered markup) may not have finished downloading and running yet -- the HTML looks complete and interactive, but nothing actually responds to events until hydration finishes.
assessments.explanation: SSR's HTML gives the page visible content immediately, but that markup has no event handlers until the JS bundle sent with it finishes downloading and running: the hydration step. Until then the page can look ready and not respond to clicks, which is the window described here. It's a normal characteristic of SSR (visible but not yet interactive), not a broken click handler or a per-click server round trip that re-renders the page.
